A merger of the Department of Landscape Architecture (LAR) with the Department of Geoscience (GEO) would join two rather small departments that share expertise in areas of great research and socio-economic importance.
Specifically, our departments address climate change issues and resilience planning, management of geological resources, including protection of drinking water resources, and urban development, such as urban flooding control.

A merger would create opportunities for sharing resources, collaborative grant applications, and, importantly, guarantees the continued accreditation of LAR.

VanderGheynst, Dean, College of the Environment and Life Sciences Re: Proposal to merge Department of Landscape Architecture and Department of Geosciences Date: November 7, 2025 ————————————————————————————————————— I fully support the proposed merger of the Department of Landscape Architecture (LAR) and the Department of Geosciences (GEO).
This merger aligns with the University’s strategic goals to strengthen interdisciplinary collaboration, enhance program sustainability, and advance our land and sea grant mission.
A budget and justification summarizing how existing resources will be used is included in the submission.
The Department of Landscape Architecture offers Rhode Island’s only accredited undergraduate program of its kind and is approaching re-accreditation in 2026.
The upcoming retirement of its two tenured faculty members would leave the program without tenured or tenure-track faculty, jeopardizing accreditation.
To ensure continuity and demonstrate institutional commitment, two tenure-track faculty searches focused on Environmental Planning and Urban Design and Transportation Planning have been approved.

The merger with Geosciences, which includes several tenured and tenure-track faculty, provides the necessary structure to support new hires and ensure compliance with Article 15 of the collective bargaining agreement.
Both departments have voted in favor of the merger, recognizing the intellectual and operational benefits of joining two small, synergistic units.
Together, they will form a hub addressing climate change, resilience planning, sustainable development, and management of natural resources.
The merged department will enhance shared teaching, research, and outreach capacity while maintaining all existing academic programs without disruption or impact on other departments or colleges.
This merger represents a forward-looking investment in programs that exemplify URI’s strengths in environmental and community-based problem solving.
It supports the continued accreditation of the Bachelor of Landscape Architecture program and positions URI as a regional leader in sustainable design and Earth system science.

Landscape Architecture Landscape architecture is a 126-credit curriculum leading to the Bachelor of Landscape Architecture (B.L.A.) degree.
Accredited by the Landscape Architecture Accreditation Board of the ASLA, the curriculum is designed to prepare undergraduates for professional careers in public and private practice.
Landscape architecture is a profession that involves the design, planning, preservation, and restoration of the landscape by applying art, science, and technology to achieve the best use of our land and water resources.
Landscape architects design and plan parks, plazas, and recreation areas; residential, institutional and commercial developments; transportation facilities, new towns and campus landscapes, and green infrastructure.
They are also involved in planning and designing landscapes in coastal areas and inland developments impacted by climate.
The requirements of this curriculum include preparation in the basic arts and sciences.

The major includes 63-64 credits of professional core classes (LAR 101, 201, 202, 243, 244, 300, 301, 302, 343, 344, 345, 346, 353, 354, 443, 444, 445, 447, 450); 28-29 credits of supporting requirements (ART 207; GEG 101; PLS 150; CHM 100, 101 or 103 or PHY 109, or GEO 100G, or 103; CPL 410, CPL 434, 538; MTH 103; and PLS 200); and 7-8 credits of supporting electives.
Students will also take general education classes and 6-7 credits of free electives.
Students accepted into landscape architecture are required to maintain a grade point average of at least 2.50 with no landscape architecture grades below a letter C.
